content: 1. An intervention was designed to enhance communication between healthcare providers and the families of hospitalized minority children. This study was published in Academic Pediatrics in 2016, volume 16, issue 5, pages 460-467. 2. O’Connor SO, Devlin AM, McGee-Lennon M, Bouamrane MM, O’Donnell CA, and Mair FS conducted a study on factors influencing participation in the eRedBook, a personal child health record. This research was presented in Nursing Informatics in 2016, pages 971-972. 3. Phipps H explored the perspectives of pregnant women on carrying their own medical records. This study was published in the Australian and New Zealand Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology. 4. Quinlivan JA, Lyons S, and Peterson RW conducted a survey study to assess the attitudes of pregnant women towards different types of medical record systems, including personally controlled electronic records, hospital-held records, and patient-held records. The findings were published in Telemedicine and e-Health in 2014, volume 20, issue 9, pages 810-815. 5. Sharp LK, Carvalho P, Southward M, Schmidt ML, Jabine LN, Stolley MR, and colleagues conducted an exploratory study on the use of electronic personal health records for childhood cancer survivors. This study was published in the Journal of Adolescent and Young Adult Oncology in 2014, volume 3, issue 3, pages 117-122. 6. Yanagisawa S, Soyano A, Igarashi H, Ura M, and Nakamura Y evaluated the impact of a maternal and child health handbook on maternal knowledge and behavior through a community-based controlled trial in rural Cambodia. The results were published in Health Policy and Planning in 2015, volume 30, issue 11, pages 1184-1192. 7. The World Health Organization (WHO) provided recommendations on the use of home-based records for maternal, newborn, and child health. These recommendations were based on a framework analysis of facilitators and barriers to the appropriate use of such records. 8. Various experts and organizations, including the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), United Nations Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA), and United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), contributed to the development and implementation of maternal and child health (MCH) programs across multiple countries, including Afghanistan, Ghana, India, Kenya, and others. 9. Aiga (2013) discussed the use of MCH handbooks for self-monitoring child nutrition status in Vietnam, while Hagiwara (2017) outlined the development of a new combined maternal and child health record book in Ghana. 10. The Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, UNICEF, and other partners organized workshops to revitalize home-based records, with presentations and case studies from countries like Ethiopia, Madagascar, and Jordan. 11. Studies and reports, such as those by Omar & Sugishita (2016) in Kenya, assessed the retention, perceived usefulness, and utilization of family health cards and MCH booklets in various settings.
